# Load budgets, failure policies and recovery

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `reliability-dependency-failures` · **Observability, Performance & Reliability** · Catalog level: senior

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S04-Q012](#S04-Q012)

<p>When a downstream dependency becomes unavailable, how should the calling service respond? Define what the user sees and how the system can recover.</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Define a bounded response to downstream failure that preserves a stated user and capacity contract.</p>

<ul>
<li>Separate demand, waiting and execution capacity before selecting a load response.</li>
<li>Design timeout, retry and circuit-breaker boundaries with explicit assumptions.</li>
<li>Connect failure and recovery signals to an actionable incident.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

- [Tracing a symptom to a limiting stage](observability-request-diagnosis.md)

<p>A slow or unavailable dependency consumes the caller’s time and capacity budget. Retry and queue decisions can shift or amplify that pressure, so start with acceptable user outcomes and finish by specifying how operators observe failure and recovery.</p>

<a id="S04-Q013"></a>

### S04-Q013 · Mechanism

<a id="S05-Q045"></a>

<p>How would you combine timeout, retry, exponential backoff and circuit-breaker decisions without creating a retry storm? Trace what happens when many callers encounter the same outage.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q013](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q013) · [S05-Q045](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q045)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q013](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q013)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Discuss timeout, retry, exponential backoff, circuit breaker and retry storms.

</div>

**[S05-Q045](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q045)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How should retry policies avoid retry storms?

</div>

**Why these source prompts share a canonical question:** Shared retry-storm policy; retain timeout, backoff and circuit-breaker constraints.

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>A retry storm is repeated attempts that amplify load during trouble. Explain how the controls interact, including the caller&#x27;s total waiting time.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Reason about bounded recovery attempts under shared dependency failure.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State the request deadline, retryable outcomes and whether repeating the operation is safe. Establish library/provider versions before relying on documented policy behavior.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Account for attempts across multiple layers, not only one client.</li>
<li>Give evidence for retry bounds and a recovery test under many callers.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Stacking retries at every layer without examining multiplied traffic.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>When would another attempt be harmful even after waiting longer?</li>
<li>How would you validate that recovery does not overload the dependency again?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S04-Q012"></a>

### S04-Q012 · Failure cases

<p>When a downstream dependency becomes unavailable, how should the calling service respond? Define what the user sees and how the system can recover.</p>

**Source:** [S04-Q012](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q012)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S04-Q012](../../sources/04-architecture-distributed-systems.md#q012)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How should a service behave when a downstream dependency is unavailable?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Unavailable may mean a fast error or a response that never arrives. Connect the chosen behavior to the operation rather than using one fallback for everything.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Design dependency-failure behavior from the user contract.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Clarify whether the dependency is required for correctness, whether the operation changes state and the allowed latency.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Distinguish failure, degraded success and an unknown outcome in the chosen workflow.</li>
<li>Specify observable recovery conditions and a test of the failure path.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Returning success with substitute data without checking whether it preserves the contract.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What changes if the dependency may have committed before the connection failed?</li>
<li>How will you know it is safe to resume normal traffic?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q047"></a>

### S01-Q047 · Trade-offs

<p>How do load balancing, caching, queues, backpressure and horizontal scaling address different load problems? Choose a response for one observed constraint.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q047](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q047)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q047](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q047)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Discuss load balancing, caching, queues, backpressure, and horizontal scaling as different responses to load.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Connect each approach to the resource or demand boundary it changes. Backpressure means limiting or slowing admission when downstream capacity cannot keep up.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Select a load response from a diagnosed constraint.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a hypothetical service with explicit latency, correctness and capacity requirements; do not assume that moving work to a queue removes its total cost.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains what the selected response changes and what pressure remains.</li>
<li>Compares an alternative and proposes evidence for capacity and failure behavior.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Presenting all five approaches as interchangeable cures for a slow system.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would happen if queued work arrived faster than workers could finish it?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S05-Q048"></a>

### S05-Q048 · Production decision

<p>How would you turn monitoring signals into an alert that helps someone resolve a real incident?</p>

**Source:** [S05-Q048](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q048)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S05-Q048](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q048)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How do monitoring and alerting connect technical symptoms to an actionable incident?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Connect the technical symptom to user or business impact, then explain what the responder should know and do. An alert must support a decision, not merely report activity.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Design actionable incident detection with a defined response and validation.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Clarify affected service, time window, ownership and response urgency; use a hypothetical incident rather than an invented personal history.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains the impact, evidence and intended next check in one alert scenario.</li>
<li>Tests detection and recovery behavior while accounting for noise and missing signals.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Choosing a threshold without defining impact, owner or response action.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you verify that the alert detects a dependency outage without firing during every normal traffic spike?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A hypothetical dependency becomes intermittently slow while incoming traffic continues. State a request deadline and acceptable outcomes, compare bounded retries with rejection or deferred work, and trace a failure plus recovery. Define a queue/admission limit and an alert that tells an operator what evidence to inspect.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Explains the mechanisms and states a coherent user-visible failure outcome.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Defends total budgets, duplicate or overload risks and recovery behavior with a validation and alert plan.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>A list of resilience patterns or “retry three times” without timing and load assumptions is insufficient.</p>
